we present a new method for the synthesis of monodispersed CdS/ZnSe nanocrystals exhibiting high quantum yields and narrow emission linewidths.
we have developed a new method for the synthesis of monodispersed CdS nanocrystallites with ZnS shell, using a combination of zinc ethylxantate (Zn(EX)2) and stearate as the ZnS precursor.
a new method for the preparation of monodispersee CdS/Zn S core/shell nanorystals has been developed.

the development of a new, facile and environmentally friendly method for the synthesis of monodispersed, highly luminescencent CdS/ZnSe core/shell nanorods (NRs) with high photoluminescence quantum yields.
the synthesis and characterization of colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs).
a new method to prepare CdS/ZnSe core/shell nanorods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Zn(ex)2 can successfully be used as precursor for the synthesis of highly luminescent and monodisperse CdS/ZnSe core/shell nanorystals.
ZnS capped CdSe/ZnS core–shell nanocrystals are a promising candidate for a variety of applications in optoelectronic devices.

this method allows for the synthesis of highly luminescent and monodisperse CdS/Zn(S,ex)2 core/shell nanorods and nanocrystals, exhibiting narrow emission linewidth of 15 nm (FWHM), with quantum yields of 35–45%.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ZnS shell formation on the surface of colloidal CdSe and CdS nanocrystal cores is a promising approach to achieve highly luminescent and stable nanocrystals with tunable emission properties.

the use of the new monomolecular precursor Zn(ex)2 for the capping with ZnS is very promising, since it allows the synthesis of high quality CdS/Zn(x)S core/shell quantum dots with very good luminescence properties.
the combination of Zn(ex)2 and zinc stearatereveals a new, efficient and safe method for the cationic exchange of CdS nanocrystallites with ZnS shells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the ZnS shell formation is not restricted to a narrow range of growth temperatures and can be performed at temperatures as low as 100 °C, which is a significant advantage over the conventional method of ZnS shell formation using bis(trimethylsiliyl) sulfide (TMS2S) and diethylzine (DEZ).
the use of a non-hazardous, air-stable and low temperature precursor (Zn(ex)) for the growth of ZnS shells is possible and leads to the synthesis of highly luminescent core/shell nanocrysals.
ZnS shells with thicknesses of 1–3 monolayers are formed by the use of Zn(ex)2, whereas thicker shells are obtained with the application of zinc stearate.
